description.narrative:
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) approved the establishment of the Urban Environmental Infrastructure Fund (UEIF) on 2 December 2009 under the Urban Financing Partnership Facility (UFPF). Parallel to this approval was the commitment of the Government of Sweden to contribute about $14 million for the UEIF, followed by an additional contribution of $7 million in 2011. The fund supports ADBs response to the huge unmet needs of the region for both basic and economic infrastructure, which under the then prevailing Strategy 2020 is a core business area of operations. The objective of UEIF is to raise and invest cofi nancing from development partner agencies to support the implementation of Strategy 2020 through the provision of grants for technical assistance and investments focused on providing propoor and/or environmental benefits.
The proposed credit facility addresses areas where Swedish companies have a high competence and are competitive. The ADB deliberately approached Sida for support within this area since Sweden is regarded to possess solid knowledge and be able to share experience.
Results to be achieved by the credit frame:
Increased financing of projects within the urban environment area
Increased cooperation with and possibility to have an impact on ADB
More effective resource allocation for preparation of projects
Increased possibilities for Swedish actors to participate in projects funded by ADB
Objectives
In the context of the need for urban environment financing, the objectives proposed should be to provide the support to cities and governments to actually implement environmental projects for which there are many unrealised plans. The support will consist of a grant component of SEK 150 million to be linked to a loan from the Bank or from other local commercial bank. The grant component ca be combined with the access to guarantees in the amount of SEK 500 million. The Sida guarantees can be used without connection to grantfinancing. The guarantees can be used to extend the repayment period of a loan or it can be a stand alone guarantee issued together with the Asian Development Bank.
The envisaged Sida financing facility to ADB for Urban Environment is complementary to and reinforces the Sida technical support to the Cities Development Initiative in Asia (CDIA) and the participation in the multidonor Clean Energy Fund (CEF). The complementary financingv facility has the following three objectives:
to maximize the impact of Swedish support in respect of promoting environmental and poverty reduction outcomes;
to make ADB-financed investment programs in urban environment more attractive to the borrower/end-user.
to minimize Sida´s transaction costs of such urban environmental and sustainable energy support.
Urban Partnership Facility with Asian Development Bank, for cofinancing of the important environmental projects in Asia. The fund is related to a guarantee fund in the amount of SEK 500 million.
Urban partnership facility hos Asiatiska utvecklingsbanken, för delfinansiering av viktiga miljöprojekt i Asien. Fondern är relaterad till en garantifond uppgående till 500 miljoner SEK.

The investment co-financing provided by the intervention has delivered results in the following areas: - (i) Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation; (ii) Urban Environmental Transportation Services; (iii) Urban Environmental Water and Wastewater Services; (iv) Urban Environmental Solid Waste Management Services; (v) District Heating and Cooling Services; and (vi) Urban Renewal.
In terms of sector allocations of the UEIF, almost half (about 46%) of the trust funds resources were provided to water supply and sanitation projects, followed by solid waste management at 28%, and most of the results fall under these areas. In total the trust fund has approved and completed 49 urban environmental infrastructure projects. The biggest share by region is the East Asia Regional Department, both in terms of project commitments of $6.48 million (33%) and number of initiatives with 13 projects implemented.
Below are some examples of results achieved:
1. Support to the Ulaanbaatar Urban Services and Ger Areas Development Investment Program in Mongolia This support aimed at enhanced operational efficiency in Ulaanbaatar water supply and wastewater services, which were under pressure following the growth of Ulaanbaatars population. The UEIF investment grant (IG) was utilized to finance a range of activities centred on improving system efficiency and reducing operational costs in water supply service delivery. These included supply and installation of energy-efficient pump equipment and a supervisory control and data acquisition system, construction and commissioning of pumping stations, establishment of the Ulaanbaatar Water Supply and Sewerage Authority (USUG) central monitoring system, and installation of monitoring and distribution wells connected to a fibre optic network.
Results from this support include efficient and reliable water service provision. The investments in the physical network enabled USUG to better manage system delivery pressure, reduce water system non-revenue water losses, and introduce more efficient energy management measures such as utilizing energy efficient pumping systems, the use of innovative treatment tools, and the use of modern energy distribution systems. This in turn also translates to more operational savings. Overall, the results achieved from these activities are two-fold: (i) a more efficient and reliable water service provision for the public; and (ii) improved fiscal standing of USUG through reduced operational costs.
2. Ulaanbaatar Air Quality Improvement Program Ulaanbaatars harsh climate and rapid and uncoordinated urban development contribute to some of the highest levels of air pollution registered worldwide, posing serious public health concerns. Main sources of health-adverse pollution include raw coal burning in inefficient stoves for heating, continuous coal burning for electricity generation and heating services in the formal urban areas, increasing motor vehicle emissions, and dust from unpaved roads. The negative impacts of pollution not only contribute to poor health outcomes such as chronic illnesses and shorter life expectancy but also to poor living standards, including high medical costs and lost productivity.
As part of this support, an expert was recruited to consult on the social and environmental impacts of proposed air pollution control policies through a qualitative and quantitative analysis of their anticipated positive and negative impacts. The intervention assisted the Government of Mongolia in reviewing feasible options for the supply of cleaner heating fuel, from sourcing to distribution. This was instrumental in creating a sustainable emergency scheme to distribute cleaner fuel to poor families in peri-urban districts, including a government resolution banning the usage of raw coal. Moreover, expert advice on safety and energy efficiency standards for the improved fuel was provided, contributing to its sustainability by ensuring safe use and demand from residents.
3. Revitalization of Informal Settlements and their Environments using a Water-Sensitive Approach The support aimed at demonstrating the effectiveness of a water-sensitive approach for wastewater treatment, flood risk reduction, and urban environment improvement using decentralized green infrastructure to biologically treat contaminated and polluted water. Lessons will inform the technical design, implementation arrangements, and cost estimates for larger-scale interventions that AsDB may undertake.
UEIF funding was utilized to engage an international design and implementation management consultant (Monash Sustainable Development Institute) and an individual national consultant to provide support at a site in Fiji.
Results and Impact: - Appropriate water-sensitive design generated. Co-design involved intensive participatory design activities with the residents at the project site. Community engagement continued during the detailed engineering drawing and construction process. - Capacity for operation and maintenance of water-sensitive infrastructure developed. Two training sessions in Fiji on water-sensitive cities approaches and green infrastructure operation and maintenance developed and delivered. These trainings benefitted nine households and 24 government representatives. - Knowledge distribution to inform the scaling up of the projects generated. The experience and lessons from implementing the pilot projects were captured and helped inform the publication of three knowledge products, which focused on co-design principles, participatory approaches, policy considerations, and technical requirements. The knowledge products were launched during a virtual event with 113 participants. A pilot demonstration activity of the water-sensitive approach was conducted in an informal settlement in Suva, Fiji. The activity resulted in the construction of seven pressure tanks, 16 bathroom units, and more than 221 m2 of constructed wetland area. This benefitted around 34 houses (182 residents).
4. Karnataka Integrated Urban Water Management Investment Program Under the overall aim to improve wastewater treatment and sewerage systems in the state of Karnataka, support was provided to improve water resource management in urban areas in a holistic and sustainable manner consistent with the principles of Integrated Water Resources Management.
Activities under the UEIF investment grant include: - the engagement of a nongovernment organization tasked to develop community-based sanitation interventions (e.g., water supplies, sewerage connections, toilets, and improved wastewater collection and treatment systems) for poor and vulnerable communities; - sanitation-related awareness targeting the urban poor; - communication on gender inclusion elements and social/environmental safeguards; - facilitating construction of household and community toilets and school toilets, including connection to the sewerage network; - facilitating the use of newly constructed household toilets; including the operation and maintenance of community toilets.
Results and Impact: -A total of 5,539 output-based toilets and new connections were provided, benefitting around 33,234 residents. An additional 54 toilets for schools and colleges were also constructed. The beneficiaries were involved in various awareness programs conducted to improve sanitation activities, which substantially helped them overcome health issues, generate behavior change, and achieve social and economic development in the community. Collectively, the program has resulted in improved quality of life in the project areas.
Support to Knowledge and Capacity Development Besides supporting AsDB projects, UEIF also supported the development of knowledge products as well as knowledge-sharing events that showcased AsDBs work on urban development in the region. Among these are:
- Urban Climate Change Resilience: A Synopsis (2014). This publication briefly introduces the core principles and qualities of urban climate change resilience, including lessons from applying this approach across South and Southeast Asian Cities.
- Incentives for Reducing Disaster Risk in Urban Areas (2016). This publication summarizes the experiences in three case study areas in Viet Nam, Nepal, and the Philippines, indicating an opportunity to leverage existing incentive and/or investment programs to encourage investment in disaster risk reduction. It explains incentive options and how they are used in the case areas to encourage investments in disaster risk reduction in developing countries.
Integrated Solid Waste Management for Local Governments: A Practical Guide (2017). This publication introduced key integrated solid waste management concepts and identified cross-cutting issues in the sector. It contains over 40 practice briefs covering solid waste management planning, waste categories, waste containers and collection, waste processing and diversion, landfill development, landfill operations, and contract issues.
The intervention has most notably contributed to the objective of providing support to cities and governments to implement environmental projects. In this regard, the assessment is that the intervention has achieved satisfactory results and has had a positive impact on the capacity of cities and governments to implement environment and poverty reduction projects. Throughout the relatively long period that the intervention has operated, the UEIF has supported urban environmental infrastructure components which notably support pro-poor and socially inclusive development and that bring environmental benefits to communities. Examples of these are increased access to sanitation facilities for women and vulnerable communities in Karnataka in India, and the piloting of nature-based solutions to upgrade community sewerage and flood control infrastructure in Makassar, Indonesia and in Suva, Fiji, among others.
However, it is Sidas assessment that not all projects under the intervention have contributed to environmental sustainability. Furthermore, for some of the objectives that the intervention set out to achieve, results are difficult to evidence. This is, at least partly, due to the fact that the intervention has run over more than 15 years, which means that supporting documentation in terms of e.g. conclusions and assessments is not always readily available.
In terms of maximising the impact of the Swedish support, it can be noted that in 2019 resources for supporting projects and TAs started to dwindle and much of the funding available was generated from savings from completed projects. The ability to reallocate trust fund savings from completed projects thus enabled new projects to be funded. Among the projects benefitting from this was the Ulaanbaatar Air Quality Improvement Program, mentioned above, helping to introduce reforms to reduce the amount of air pollution in the city.
The support for the UEIF and the collaboration with AsDB has also contributed to further collaboration with the AsDB in the form of a guarantee collaboration for AsDB:s Innovative Finance Facility for Climate in Asia and the Pacific (IF-CAP).
The UEIF is also considered to have provided a strong foundation to other trust funds that at a later stage were set up under the UFPF umbrella. A further three trust funds, with a stronger climate focus, were established under the UFPF umbrella: the Urban Climate Change Resilience Trust Fund, Cities Development Initiative for Asia Trust Fund, and ASEAN Australia Smart Cities Trust Fund.
The support for the UEIF was part of larger collection of infrastructure intervention efforts agreed by Sida, such as PIDG and the IFC, with the aim of strengthening capacity and building knowledge as well as increasing infrastructure investments. This larger effort has however not been comprehensively evaluated, and therefore no conclusions can be drawn around the UEIF support contribution to this holistic intervention approach towards infrastructure investments.
Sweden was the only donor to the UEIF, and all projects have therefore now been completed and the Fund will not continue in its current form.
Financial results and fund usage
Between 2009 and 2022, in total UEIF supported 49 AsDB projects across AsDB operations, with the biggest share by region going to the East Asia Regional Department, both in terms of funds committed to projects with a total of $6.48 million (37%) and the number of initiatives with 13 projects implemented.
As of September 2024, total UEIF commitments (net of savings generated from closed funding activities) amounted to $17.34 million, including $2.52 million for direct charge activities, $7.00 million for TA, and $7.82 million for investment grants. These commitments constitute a total of 49 projects and activities, including 24 direct charge activities, 19 TA projects, and six investment grants. In terms of the amount of ADB projects that were leveraged using UEIF resources, an estimated total value of $2.1 billion worth of loan investments approved and committed by ADB was reached. No Sida guarantee has been initiated in conjunction with the UEIF collaboration.
At final accounting of the UEIF resources, the total amount remitted back to Sida amounted to $3.84 million, including $1.11 million on interests earned. Sida received the said amount, or 41 879 100,86 SEK, on December 9, 2024 med noteringen "Funds are from ADB - UEIF code 5402".
Seemingly one key result from the contribution, is how Sida's support to the UEIF and the deepened collaboration with AsDB has contributed to further collaboration with the AsDB in the form of the guarantee collaboration around AsDB:s IF-CAP. This Sida guarantee agreement of $200 million, set to mobilize some $10 144 million in capital for climate financing, is set to be signed in early 2025. This will be one Sida's largest guarantees in terms of guarantee amount and the additional lending it will generate.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
